lessonTitle: McDonald’s: A World of Tasty Twists
level: OFS Grade 9 International English G1/G2 ESL
lessonGoal: Students identify how a global restaurant brand adapts to local cultures, distinguish source claims from examples, and write an evidence-based explanation of why local adaptation can matter in global business.

warmUp.title: Warm-up
warmUp.instructions: Discuss these warm-up questions with a partner. Think about your own experiences with international foods and global brands.
questions: What kinds of food or products change from country to country?
Why might a global restaurant change its menu or service in different places?
What is the difference between a local idea and a global business?

article.title: McDonald’s: A World of Tasty Twists
article.sourceNote: Original text transcribed from one teacher-provided classroom image. The visible source label is “Source: CNN”; no publication date or article URL is shown in the image.
paragraphs: Did you know that McDonald’s has over 42,000 restaurants serving 65 million people each day? That’s nearly the entire population of the United Kingdom eating McDonald’s on the same day. A new book called McAtlas by photojournalist Gary He shows that McDonald’s actually changes a lot depending on where you are.

Gary He traveled to more than 55 countries to see these changes for himself. In India, where many people don’t eat beef, McDonald’s created entirely new menu lines, like the Big Spicy McWrap Paneer and the McAloo Tikki burger. In Sweden, one location lets you ski right up to the window to order. It’s called McSki, and it’s the only ski-through McDonald’s on Earth. In Israel, where kosher rules are followed, you won’t find cheeseburgers, but you can order a burger made from prime rib instead!
According to He, this local creativity is the secret behind the brand’s global success. “Without adjusting to local tastes,” he says, “you couldn’t do business globally.”

mainIdeaQuestion.question: What is the main idea of the article?
options: McDonald’s serves exactly the same menu and service in every country.
McDonald’s changes some menus and experiences to fit local cultures while operating as a global brand.
Only people in India eat food from McDonald’s.
A photojournalist can succeed only by visiting one country.

feedback.correct: O Correct! The article shows that McDonald's operates globally but adapts menus and services—such as vegetarian lines in India, McSki in Sweden, and kosher choices in Israel—to match local cultures.
feedback.incorrect: X Incorrect. Option B is correct because the article explains how McDonald's combines global reach with local cultural adaptations across different nations.

mainIdeaQuestion.explanation: Paragraph 1 establishes the enormous global scale of McDonald’s with over 42,000 restaurants, Paragraph 2 provides concrete examples of cultural adaptation in India, Sweden, and Israel, and Paragraph 3 quotes Gary He explaining that local creativity and adapting to local tastes are the secret behind the brand's global success.

evidenceFromText.title: Evidence from the Text
evidenceFromText.instructions: Respond to each prompt using specific facts and details directly from the article. Click 'Check & Compare' to evaluate your work against model responses.

prompts.statement: What evidence shows that McDonald’s changes according to the country or local culture?
compareTips: Identify specific country adaptations from the reading (India, Sweden, Israel).
Reference Gary He's documentation in his book McAtlas across 55+ countries.
Note specific menu items or service formats (vegetarian lines, McSki, kosher rules).
prompts.modelAnswer: The article provides concrete evidence that McDonald's alters its offerings depending on geography. In India, where many people do not eat beef, the brand created new vegetarian lines like the Big Spicy McWrap Paneer and McAloo Tikki burger. In Sweden, it opened McSki, the world's only ski-through location. In Israel, it follows kosher dietary rules by omitting cheeseburgers and offering prime rib burgers instead. Photojournalist Gary He observed and documented these variations by visiting more than 55 countries for his book McAtlas.

prompts.statement: Compare the India, Sweden and Israel examples from the article. What is different about each one?
compareTips: Contrast the type of adaptation in each location (dietary tradition vs. physical climate vs. religious rules).
Mention India's beef-free menu additions (paneer wrap, potato burger).
Mention Israel's kosher rule compliance (no cheeseburgers, prime rib burger available).
prompts.modelAnswer: The three examples highlight distinct forms of local adaptation. In India, the adaptation is dietary and cultural: because many citizens avoid beef, McDonald's introduced unique vegetarian items such as the Big Spicy McWrap Paneer. In contrast, the Swedish adaptation is architectural and environmental: McSki allows winter sports enthusiasts to ski directly to the ordering window. In Israel, the adaptation is religious and regulatory: locations follow kosher laws by excluding cheeseburgers while introducing a premium prime rib burger.

prompts.statement: How does Gary He’s quotation explain the connection between local tastes and global business?
compareTips: Quote or reference Gary He's concluding statement: 'Without adjusting to local tastes, you couldn't do business globally.'
Explain that local creativity is identified as the secret behind the brand's global success.
Emphasize that global companies must respect regional cultural preferences to remain viable.
prompts.modelAnswer: Gary He's quotation directly connects local cultural awareness with international commercial viability. He states, 'Without adjusting to local tastes, you couldn't do business globally,' and identifies this local creativity as the secret behind McDonald's global success. His statement explains that even a massive global brand cannot rely on a uniform menu; it must respect regional culinary traditions and practical lifestyles to succeed in competitive international markets.

languageFocus.title: Language Focus
languageFocus.instructions: Examine how global culture articles use specific sentence patterns to report findings, present contrasts, and express cause-and-effect relationships.

patterns.name: Source Attribution & Reporting Phrases
patterns.explanation: Writers use phrases like 'According to He' or 'shows that' to credit specific authors, photojournalists, or sources without presenting claims as universal dogma.
patterns.example: According to He, this local creativity is the secret behind the brand’s global success.
patterns.sourceExample: A new book called McAtlas by photojournalist Gary He shows that McDonald’s actually changes a lot...

patterns.name: Relative Clauses of Place & Reason
patterns.explanation: Clauses beginning with 'where' provide essential cultural or environmental background explaining why an adaptation exists.
patterns.example: In India, where many people don’t eat beef, McDonald’s created entirely new menu lines...
patterns.sourceExample: In Israel, where kosher rules are followed, you won’t find cheeseburgers...

patterns.name: Contrast & Concession Connectors
patterns.explanation: Connectors like 'whereas', 'but', and 'while' contrast different regional practices or show unexpected alternatives.
patterns.example: ...you won’t find cheeseburgers, but you can order a burger made from prime rib instead!
patterns.sourceExample: In Sweden, customers ski to the window, whereas in Israel, menus accommodate kosher traditions.

patterns.name: Negative Condition / Cause & Effect
patterns.explanation: Prepositional phrases with 'without + -ing' establish a necessary condition or warn of negative consequences.
patterns.example: “Without adjusting to local tastes,” he says, “you couldn’t do business globally.”
patterns.sourceExample: Without local creativity, global restaurant brands cannot maintain long-term success.

writingTask.title: Final Writing Task
writingTask.instructions: Draft an evidence-based explanation paragraph adhering strictly to the prompt, rubric criteria, and 100–140 word count range.
writingTask.prompt: How does McDonald’s adapt to local cultures while remaining a global brand? Write an evidence-based explanation paragraph of 100–140 words. Use at least three accurate details from the article, include examples from at least two countries, explain the connection between local tastes and global business, and end with a clear conclusion.
checklist: at least three accurate details from the original article
examples from at least two countries
correct use of the India, Sweden or Israel examples
one source-reporting phrase such as According to the article, ...
explanation of local adaptation and global business
100–140 words; no invented statistics, dates or outside examples presented as article facts
writingTask.modelAnswer: A successful multinational brand must balance global scale with localized customer experiences. According to the article, McDonald’s operates over 42,000 restaurants serving 65 million people daily, yet it alters its operations significantly across different regions. In India, where many people avoid beef, the company introduced vegetarian items like the Big Spicy McWrap Paneer and McAloo Tikki burger. Meanwhile, Sweden features McSki, a ski-through location adapted to local snowy conditions. Furthermore, locations in Israel observe kosher rules by omitting cheeseburgers and offering prime rib instead. As photojournalist Gary He concludes, adjusting to local tastes is vital because global business cannot survive without regional flexibility. In conclusion, respecting local culture enables a global corporation to thrive worldwide.

teacherNotes: 1. THREE-PARAGRAPH PROGRESSION: Note the macro-structure of the reading text. Paragraph 1 introduces global scale and photojournalist Gary He's thesis; Paragraph 2 presents three concrete country case studies (India, Sweden, Israel); Paragraph 3 synthesizes these examples with Gary He's concluding principle on global business survival.

2. DISTINCTION BETWEEN GLOBAL SCALE AND LOCAL ADAPTATION: Emphasize to students that McDonald's does not abandon its global identity. Rather, it maintains corporate systems and scale (42,000 restaurants) while innovating locally to respect distinct cultural practices.

3. SOURCE-BASED EVIDENCE VS. OUTSIDE OPINION: Remind students that all claims and examples must derive strictly from the CNN article text. Do not allow students to invent other national menus (e.g. teriyaki burgers in Japan or bulgogi burgers in Korea) when writing evidence-based paragraphs.

4. ATTRIBUTION TO GARY HE: Point out that Gary He is the author of McAtlas and the primary investigative source cited by CNN. Teach students how journalists use third-party experts to support news features.

5. MEANING OF 'LOCAL TASTES': Clarify that 'local tastes' encompasses not only flavor preferences (spiciness, sweetness) but also religious dietary laws (kosher, vegetarian traditions) and geographic lifestyles (skiing culture).

6. INDIA CASE STUDY (VEGETARIAN INNOVATION): Highlight that cultural dietary restrictions (avoiding beef) prompted positive culinary innovation—creating brand new items like Big Spicy McWrap Paneer and McAloo Tikki—rather than business withdrawal.

7. SWEDEN CASE STUDY (ENVIRONMENTAL/SERVICE ADAPTATION): Contrast Sweden's McSki with menu adaptations. Here, the adaptation is physical architecture and service delivery tailored to a snowy recreational lifestyle.

8. ISRAEL CASE STUDY & NEUTRAL TREATMENT OF KOSHER RULES: Present kosher rules respectfully and objectively as traditional Jewish dietary guidelines (e.g. prohibiting the mixing of dairy and meat, which excludes cheeseburgers). Note that McDonald's offered a prime rib alternative instead.

9. EVALUATING SOURCE NUMBERS CAUTIOUSLY: Emphasize that figures like 'over 42,000 restaurants' and '65 million people' are reported by the source as approximate daily totals. Teach students to use qualifying language ('According to the article', 'The source states') rather than declaring absolute timeless facts.

10. ESL SCAFFOLDING FOR COMPARISON & EVIDENCE: For G1/G2 ESL learners, provide sentence stems comparing contrasts (e.g. 'While customers in Sweden can ski to the window, customers in Israel select kosher options...'). Break down compound-complex sentences into manageable chunks before drafting.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Did you know that McDonald’s has over 42,000 restaurants serving 65 million people each day?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Did you know / that McDonald’s has / over 42,000 restaurants / serving 65 million people / each day?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 당신은 알고 있었나요 / 맥도날드가 가지고 있다는 것을 / 42,000개 이상의 레스토랑을 / 6,500만 명의 사람들에게 음식을 제공하는 / 매일?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 맥도날드가 매일 6,500만 명의 사람들에게 음식을 제공하는 42,000개 이상의 매장을 운영하고 있다는 사실을 알고 계셨나요?

mustKnowChunks.example: The global brand has over 42,000 restaurants across dozens of countries.
The transportation system moves millions of commuters each day.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Rhetorical introductory question ('Did you know that...') with noun clause; present participial modifier ('serving 65 million people...') providing ongoing descriptive data; preposition 'over' used as a numerical approximation.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Think about how big McDonald’s is. / It has more than 42,000 locations worldwide. / Every single day, / 65 million people eat there. / That shows its massive global scale.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 맥도날드가 얼마나 큰지 상상해 보세요. / 전 세계에 42,000개가 넘는 매장이 있습니다. / 매일매일 / 6,500만 명의 사람들이 그곳에서 식사합니다. / 이는 엄청난 세계적 규모를 보여줍니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Notice how the author opens with a rhetorical question to hook the reader with mind-boggling numbers.
teachingTranscript.korean: 작가가 독자의 흥미를 끌기 위해 엄청난 숫자를 담은 수사 의문문으로 글을 시작한다는 점에 주목하세요.

teachingTranscript.english: What does 'serving' do here? It acts as an active participle describing what those 42,000 restaurants do every day.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'serving'은 여기서 무엇을 하나요? 42,000개 매장이 매일 하는 일을 설명하는 능동 분사 역할을 합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Check: How many people are served daily? 65 million people.
teachingTranscript.korean: 확인: 매일 몇 명에게 음식이 제공되나요? 6,500만 명입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Correction: Be careful not to confuse 42,000 restaurants with the 65 million customers who eat there.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교정: 42,000개 매장 수와 그곳에서 식사하는 6,500만 명의 고객 수를 혼동하지 않도록 주의하세요.

sentenceAnalysis.original: That’s nearly the entire population of the United Kingdom eating McDonald’s on the same day.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: That’s nearly / the entire population / of the United Kingdom / eating McDonald’s / on the same day.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 그것은 거의 / 전체 인구입니다 / 영국의 / 맥도날드를 먹는 / 같은 날에.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 그것은 영국 전체 인구에 가까운 사람들이 같은 날 맥도날드를 먹는 것과 같은 규모입니다.

mustKnowChunks.example: The stadium held nearly the entire population of the small town.
Millions of citizens cast their votes on the same day.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Demonstrative pronoun 'That' referring to the 65 million daily customers; adverb 'nearly' qualifying the adjective 'entire'; participial phrase 'eating McDonald’s' modifying the population noun phrase.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: To picture 65 million people, / think of the whole United Kingdom. / That is like everyone in the UK / having a McDonald’s meal / on the very same day.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 6,500만 명이 얼마나 많은지 상상해 보려면 / 영국 전체를 떠올려 보세요. / 그것은 영국에 사는 모든 사람이 / 정확히 같은 날에 / 맥도날드 식사를 하는 것과 같습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Why does the writer mention the United Kingdom here? To give readers a familiar mental picture of 65 million people.
teachingTranscript.korean: 작가가 왜 여기서 영국을 언급했을까요? 독자들에게 6,500만 명이 얼마나 되는지 친숙한 비교 대상을 주기 위해서입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Notice the word 'nearly'—it shows that 65 million is close to, but not exactly, the UK population.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'nearly'라는 단어를 보세요—6,500만 명이 영국 인구에 가깝지만 완전히 동일하지는 않다는 신중한 표현입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Check: What country's population is compared to daily McDonald's customers? The United Kingdom.
teachingTranscript.korean: 확인: 매일 맥도날드 고객 수와 비교된 나라는 어디인가요? 영국입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Correction: Note that the article does not claim all UK citizens actually eat McDonald's; it uses them as a scale comparison.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교정: 기사가 영국 국민 전체가 실제로 맥도날드를 먹는다고 주장하는 것이 아니라 규모 비교로 사용했음을 주의하세요.

sentenceAnalysis.original: A new book called McAtlas by photojournalist Gary He shows that McDonald’s actually changes a lot depending on where you are.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: A new book called McAtlas / by photojournalist Gary He / shows that McDonald’s / actually changes a lot / depending on where you are.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: McAtlas라고 불리는 새 책은 / 사진기자 게리 허에 의한 / 보여줍니다 / 맥도날드가 실제로 많이 바뀐다는 것을 / 당신이 어디에 있는지에 따라.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 사진기자 게리 허의 신간 'McAtlas'는 맥도날드가 여러분이 어디에 있는지에 따라 실제로 많은 변화를 보인다는 사실을 보여줍니다.

mustKnowChunks.use: agent prepositional phrase identifying the author
mustKnowChunks.example: The documentary by photojournalist Gary He won multiple international awards.

mustKnowChunks.use: dependent preposition phrase with indirect question clause
mustKnowChunks.example: Weather conditions vary greatly depending on where you are in the mountains.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Past participle modifier 'called McAtlas'; reporting verb 'shows' taking a that-noun clause; dependent preposition 'depending on' followed by an adverbial relative/interrogative clause ('where you are').
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: A photographer named Gary He / wrote a book called McAtlas. / His book shows something surprising: / McDonald’s is not the same everywhere. / It changes / depending on the country.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 게리 허라는 사진작가가 / 'McAtlas'라는 책을 썼습니다. / 그의 책은 놀라운 사실을 보여줍니다. / 맥도날드는 어디서나 똑같지 않습니다. / 나라에 따라 / 실제로 많은 것이 바뀝니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Look at the title of the book: 'McAtlas.' What does that combine? 'McDonald's' and 'atlas'—a map book of the world!
teachingTranscript.korean: 책 제목인 'McAtlas'를 보세요. 무엇이 합쳐진 말일까요? 'McDonald's'와 세계 지도책을 뜻하는 'atlas'입니다!

teachingTranscript.english: Notice the phrase 'depending on where you are.' It sets up the central claim that McDonald's adapts locally.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'depending on where you are'라는 구문을 보세요. 맥도날드가 지역에 따라 변화한다는 중심 주장을 설정합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Check: Who wrote the book McAtlas? Photojournalist Gary He.
teachingTranscript.korean: 확인: 책 McAtlas를 쓴 사람은 누구인가요? 사진기자 게리 허입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Correction: Gary He is a photojournalist who authored a book, not an official spokesperson for McDonald's.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교정: 게리 허는 책을 집필한 사진기자이지 맥도날드의 공식 대변인이 아니라는 점을 분명히 하세요.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Gary He traveled to more than 55 countries to see these changes for himself.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Gary He traveled / to more than 55 countries / to see these changes / for himself.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 게리 허는 여행했습니다 / 55개국 이상으로 / 이러한 변화들을 보기 위해 / 직접.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 게리 허는 이러한 변화들을 직접 확인하기 위해 55개국 이상을 여행했습니다.

mustKnowChunks.example: The research team visited more than 55 countries to collect water samples.
The scientist wanted to observe the glacier melting for himself.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Simple past tense 'traveled' indicating completed historical action; infinitive of purpose 'to see these changes'; reflexive idiom 'for himself' expressing firsthand personal observation.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Gary He did not just guess / from his office. / He got on planes / and visited over 55 countries. / He wanted to see / every local McDonald’s / with his own eyes.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 게리 허는 사무실에서 / 그냥 짐작만 한 것이 아닙니다. / 그는 비행기를 타고 / 55개국 이상을 직접 방문했습니다. / 그는 각 지역의 맥도날드를 / 자기 눈으로 직접 / 보고 싶었습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: What does 'for himself' mean here? It means he didn't rely on second-hand internet rumors—he experienced it in person.
teachingTranscript.korean: 여기서 'for himself'는 무슨 뜻일까요? 인터넷 소문에 의존하지 않고 그가 직접 현장을 경험했다는 뜻입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Look at the number: 'more than 55 countries.' This shows the breadth of evidence behind his conclusions.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'more than 55 countries'라는 숫자를 보세요. 그의 결론 뒤에 있는 광범위한 증거를 보여줍니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Check: Why did Gary He travel to so many countries? To see the changes for himself.
teachingTranscript.korean: 확인: 게리 허는 왜 그렇게 많은 나라를 여행했나요? 변화를 직접 확인하기 위해서입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Correction: Notice the preposition 'to'—he traveled *to* more than 55 countries, not *for* 55 years.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교정: 전치사 'to'를 주목하세요—55년 동안이 아니라 55개국 이상으로 여행했다는 뜻입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: In India, where many people don’t eat beef, McDonald’s created entirely new menu lines, like the Big Spicy McWrap Paneer and the McAloo Tikki burger.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: In India, / where many people don’t eat beef, / McDonald’s created / entirely new menu lines, / like the Big Spicy McWrap Paneer / and the McAloo Tikki burger.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 인도에서, / 많은 사람들이 소고기를 먹지 않는, / 맥도날드는 만들었습니다 / 완전히 새로운 메뉴 라인들을, / 빅 스파이시 맥랩 파니르와 같은 / 그리고 맥알루 티키 버거와 같은.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 많은 사람들이 소고기를 먹지 않는 인도에서, 맥도날드는 빅 스파이시 맥랩 파니르나 맥알루 티키 버거와 같은 완전히 새로운 메뉴 라인을 개발했습니다.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: where many people don’t eat beef
mustKnowChunks.use: non-defining relative clause explaining cultural context
mustKnowChunks.example: In cultures where many people don’t eat beef, restaurants offer vegetarian options.
The bakery developed entirely new menu lines using gluten-free flour.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Non-defining relative clause beginning with relative adverb 'where' providing cultural background; past tense 'created'; adverb 'entirely' modifying adjective 'new'; preposition 'like' introducing specific proper noun examples.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: In India, many people / do not eat beef / because of their traditions. / So what did McDonald’s do? / They did not give up. / They created brand-new vegetarian foods / made with paneer cheese and potatoes.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 인도에서는 많은 사람들이 / 문화적 전통 때문에 / 소고기를 먹지 않습니다. / 맥도날드는 어떻게 했을까요? / 포기하지 않았습니다. / 파니르 치즈와 감자로 만든 / 완전히 새로운 채식 메뉴를 개발했습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Look at the relative clause 'where many people don’t eat beef.' It explains *why* McDonald's had to innovate.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'where many people don’t eat beef'라는 관계사절을 보세요. 맥도날드가 왜 혁신해야만 했는지 이유를 설명합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Notice the specific menu names: 'Big Spicy McWrap Paneer' and 'McAloo Tikki burger.' Paneer is an Indian cheese, and aloo means potato!
teachingTranscript.korean: 구체적 메뉴 이름들을 보세요. 'Big Spicy McWrap Paneer'와 'McAloo Tikki burger'입니다. 파니르는 인도식 치즈이고, 알루는 감자를 뜻합니다!

teachingTranscript.english: Check: What menu lines did McDonald's create in India? The Big Spicy McWrap Paneer and McAloo Tikki burger.
teachingTranscript.korean: 확인: 맥도날드가 인도에서 개발한 메뉴 라인은 무엇인가요? 빅 스파이시 맥랩 파니르와 맥알루 티키 버거입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Correction: Remember that McDonald's created *new* lines rather than just removing items; it actively designed vegetarian alternatives.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교정: 단순히 메뉴를 뺀 것이 아니라 적극적으로 새로운 채식 대안을 개발했다는 점을 기억하세요.

sentenceAnalysis.original: In Sweden, one location lets you ski right up to the window to order.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: In Sweden, / one location lets you / ski right up / to the window / to order.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 스웨덴에서, / 한 매장은 당신으로 하여금 하게 합니다 / 바로 스키를 타고 오도록 / 창문까지 / 주문하기 위해.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 스웨덴에서는 한 매장에서 주문하기 위해 창문 바로 앞까지 스키를 타고 갈 수 있게 해 줍니다.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: lets you ski right up to the window
mustKnowChunks.meaning: 창문 바로 앞까지 스키를 타고 오게 해 주다
mustKnowChunks.use: causative verb phrase with directional adverb 'right up'
mustKnowChunks.example: The beachfront cafe lets you walk right up to the counter in sandals.
Customers line up at the counter to order breakfast.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Causative verb 'lets' taking bare infinitive 'ski'; directional intensifier 'right up to'; infinitive of purpose 'to order'.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Sweden gets lots of snow. / People there love skiing. / So one McDonald’s / lets customers ski right up / to the ordering window! / You do not even / take off your skis.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 스웨덴에는 눈이 많이 내립니다. / 사람들은 스키 타는 것을 좋아하죠. / 그래서 한 맥도날드 매장은 / 손님들이 주문 창문 바로 앞까지 / 스키를 타고 오게 해 줍니다! / 스키를 벗을 필요조차 없습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Notice how this adaptation is different from India. India adapted the food; Sweden adapted the way customers physically arrive!
teachingTranscript.korean: 이 적응이 인도와 어떻게 다른지 보세요. 인도는 음식을 바꿨지만, 스웨덴은 손님이 물리적으로 도착하는 방식을 바꿨습니다!

teachingTranscript.english: Look at the structure: 'lets you ski.' The verb 'let' takes an object and a base verb without 'to.'
teachingTranscript.korean: 'lets you ski' 구조를 보세요. 사역동사 'let'은 목적어 뒤에 'to' 없는 원형부정사를 취합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Check: What can customers do at the Sweden location? Ski right up to the window to order.
teachingTranscript.korean: 확인: 스웨덴 매장에서 고객들은 무엇을 할 수 있나요? 주문 창문 바로 앞까지 스키를 타고 갈 수 있습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Correction: Notice that it says 'one location' in Sweden, not every single McDonald's in the entire country.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교정: 스웨덴 전국 매장이 아니라 '한 매장(one location)'이라고 명시되어 있음에 주의하세요.

sentenceAnalysis.original: It’s called McSki, and it’s the only ski-through McDonald’s on Earth.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: It’s called McSki, / and it’s the only / ski-through McDonald’s / on Earth.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 그것은 McSki라고 불립니다, / 그리고 그것은 유일한 것입니다 / 스키스루 맥도날드 / 지구상에서.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 그곳은 'McSki'라고 불리며, 지구상에서 유일한 스키스루 맥도날드 매장입니다.

mustKnowChunks.example: The resort opened the only ski-through coffee shop in the region.
This national park is the only place on Earth where these trees grow.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Passive structure 'is called'; coordinate clause joined by 'and'; unique modifier 'the only' with compound noun 'ski-through McDonald’s'; prepositional phrase 'on Earth'.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: This special store / has a fun name: McSki. / Instead of a drive-through for cars, / it is a ski-through for skiers. / It is the only one / anywhere in the world.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이 특별한 매장은 / 'McSki'라는 재미있는 이름을 가지고 있습니다. / 자동차를 위한 드라이브스루 대신 / 스키어를 위한 스키스루입니다. / 전 세계 어디에도 없는 / 유일한 매장입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Where does the word 'ski-through' come from? It's a creative play on 'drive-through'!
teachingTranscript.korean: 'ski-through'라는 단어는 어디서 유래했을까요? 'drive-through(드라이브스루)'를 재치 있게 변형한 말입니다!

teachingTranscript.english: Notice the phrase 'on Earth.' It emphasizes the complete uniqueness of this Swedish franchise location.

sentenceFrames: According to the article, McDonald’s operates over 42,000 restaurants, yet it alters its menus significantly in different nations.
In India, where many people don't eat beef, the brand created new vegetarian lines such as the Big Spicy McWrap Paneer.
In Sweden, customers can ski right up to the McSki order window, whereas in Israel, locations observe kosher rules.
As photojournalist Gary He explains, local creativity is vital because without adjusting to local tastes, a brand cannot do business globally.
In conclusion, adapting to local cultures enables a global corporation to thrive in competitive international markets.
paragraphOutline: 1. Topic Sentence: State how global brands balance international scale with local cultural adaptation.
2. Source Evidence (Scale): Cite McDonald's massive reach (over 42,000 restaurants serving 65 million people daily).
3. Regional Example 1: Detail India's vegetarian menu lines (Big Spicy McWrap Paneer, McAloo Tikki) where beef is avoided.
4. Regional Example 2 or 3: Contrast Sweden's McSki or Israel's kosher menu accommodations.
5. Business Connection: Cite Gary He's insight that local creativity and adapting to local tastes are essential for global success.
6. Concluding Sentence: Summarize why cultural flexibility enables sustainable international commerce.

commonMistakes.mistake: McDonalds serve the same beef burgers in India because it is global company.
commonMistakes.correction: McDonald's created entirely new vegetarian lines in India, where many people do not eat beef.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gary He said you can do business without adjusting to local taste.
commonMistakes.correction: Gary He stated that without adjusting to local tastes, you couldn't do business globally.

commonMistakes.mistake: In Sweden everyone ski to work every day.
commonMistakes.correction: In Sweden, one specific location called McSki lets customers ski right up to the ordering window.

commonMistakes.mistake: Because kosher rules are followed so cheeseburgers are banned in all countries.
commonMistakes.correction: Because kosher rules are followed in Israel, McDonald's does not serve cheeseburgers there, but offers prime rib instead.

teacherCorrectionFocus: Check that students do not invent menus from unmentioned countries (e.g. Korea, Japan, Mexico).
Verify that at least three accurate source details and two country examples are clearly presented.
Ensure attribution phrases ('According to the article', 'As Gary He explains') are punctuated correctly.
Check that the final paragraph word count is strictly between 100 and 140 words.
